home.lead: GFIC Crew (known in Chinese as GFIC歪果社) is a growing real-life social community for expats in China. Founded by locals who know the country well, we are dedicated to helping global friends live a fun, connected, and hassle-free life here. We're starting in Guangzhou and Shenzhen, and expats anywhere in China can join our online groups and our national group. Here's what we're building towards: social events, parties, and meetups: everything from rooftop parties, BBQs, karaoke nights, wine tastings, and club nights to networking mixers, food crawls, language exchanges, hikes, sports leagues, Chinese cultural experiences, weekend getaways, and more.
home.title: Life happens face to face.

site.tagline: A real-life social community for expats in China.
site.description: GFIC Crew (GFIC歪果社) is a growing real-life social community for expats in China, founded by locals who know the country well. We meet up in person in Guangzhou and Shenzhen, and we run online groups plus a national group that expats in any Chinese city can join. We keep ten meetup formats on the board, from parties and networking mixers to food crawls, language exchange and weekend getaways.

rules: Show respect for the diverse cultures of all countries and prohibit any discriminatory remarks based on race, gender, religion, or any other grounds.
Prohibit commercial advertisements to ensure a positive and supportive atmosphere within the crew.
Strictly forbid any illegal activities or remarks.
Don't harass or add other crew members as friends without their consent.

formats.why: No shared hobby and no structured activity to sit through, so the party does the work for you. Rooftop parties, BBQs, karaoke nights, wine tastings, club nights, and themed or holiday nights all put people in the same room with something to do. That is why they are both an easy way in and the thing people keep coming back to.
formats.name: Parties and socials
formats.inChina: The party is familiar, the surroundings are not. Which venues are used to international crowds, what a night actually costs, how to get home afterwards, and how to find the crowd in the first place. Someone who already knows skips the part where you guess.
formats.tagline: The format everyone already knows how to enjoy.
formats.soloNote: Turning up alone is normal here, not awkward: almost everyone at a party is there to meet people. Coming in with the crew means you are never the one left by the door.

formats.why: A mixer gives you a reason to talk to a stranger before you have one: work, a side project, or simply being new in town. It suits people who would rather have a stated purpose than a purely social night, and it is where a lot of the practical help in the community first gets passed around.
formats.name: Networking mixers
formats.inChina: Industry events happen in every big Chinese city, but they are scattered, often run in Chinese, and hard to find from the outside. A crew mixer pulls the same expat and internationally-minded crowd into one room and handles the introductions.
formats.tagline: A room where everyone is there to meet someone new.
formats.soloNote: Everyone arrives alone, so there is nothing to explain. The whole point of the format is that you do not know anyone yet.

formats.why: Eating together is the one thing every culture already agrees on. You point, you react, and that reaction becomes the conversation. Hands-on food like hotpot or dumplings works better than a formal dinner because everyone is busy doing something.
formats.name: Food crawls and shared meals
formats.inChina: The food is why plenty of people came to China, but ordering it is a separate skill. Pictureless menus, dishes you cannot pronounce, and no reliable way to tell whether you chose well. Having someone order for the table turns a stressful meal into a good one.
formats.tagline: Nobody has to be interesting when there is food on the table.
formats.soloNote: Eating alone is normal at home and draws attention in a lot of Chinese restaurants. Going with people removes the stares and gets you more dishes to try.

formats.why: Saying you are here to practice Chinese is a much easier sentence than saying you are here to meet people. That is why quieter people turn up to these and never turn up to anything else. It also brings two crowds into one room: expats who want Chinese and locals who want English.
formats.name: Language exchange
formats.inChina: Demand is enormous and quality is uneven. Plenty of people have been to one that quietly became a dating event, or an English corner where nobody talks to anyone new. Sessions with a host, a structure and a topic are rare enough that you notice straight away.
formats.tagline: A reason to show up that is easier to say out loud than wanting friends.
formats.soloNote: Almost nobody feels awkward arriving alone here, because the whole point is that you get paired with someone within minutes.

formats.why: Time is the thing that turns acquaintances into friends. On a day trip there is room for the conversation to get past where you are from and what you do. People who move here often arrive already liking the outdoors, so there is nothing to sell.
formats.name: Hikes and weekend getaways
formats.inChina: There is a lot of scenery within reach of every big Chinese city, and getting to it means tickets, transport, sometimes a night somewhere, and a language gap at each step. Doing that alone on a Saturday is a big ask, which is why most people never do.
formats.tagline: A whole day together does more than an evening does.
formats.soloNote: Nobody joins a hike to talk to people they already know. Turning up alone is the normal way to do it.

formats.why: Sport gives you a job on the pitch and something to talk about afterwards, so language stops being the barrier. The repeat factor is what sets it apart though. You see the same faces regularly instead of once, and that is how friendships actually form.
formats.name: Sports leagues and fitness
formats.inChina: Courts and pitches are everywhere in Chinese cities. What eats your time is rounding up enough people, holding a booking, and making sure somebody comes next week. Most informal attempts fade out after two sessions for exactly this reason.
formats.tagline: You can be useful before your Mandarin is good enough for small talk.
formats.soloNote: Turning up alone is expected. Teams are short of players far more often than they are full.

formats.why: Real interest in Chinese culture is common and hard to follow up on your own. You have to find someone who teaches it, get there, and then work out what you are actually looking at. In a session like this all of that is handled, and there are other people reacting alongside you.
formats.name: Chinese cultural experiences
formats.inChina: Being run by locals is the genuine edge here. A Chinese host explaining dumplings, calligraphy or tea is not putting on a show for visitors, they are explaining something they grew up with, and people pick up on that difference immediately.
formats.tagline: Curiosity is easy. Acting on it alone is not.
formats.soloNote: These are structured enough that you are never left standing in a corner wondering who to talk to.

formats.why: Structure is the whole appeal. Nobody has to improvise small talk because there is something on the table that everyone is looking at. It suits people who are new in town, or who are not going to walk up to a stranger and introduce themselves.
formats.name: Board games and trivia nights
formats.inChina: It needs games in English and most shops stock Chinese versions, so somebody has to bring them. That takes a bit more setup than a night out, so it takes longer to get going.
formats.tagline: The game supplies the conversation so you do not have to.
formats.soloNote: Good first event. You spend the first twenty minutes learning rules rather than making conversation.

formats.why: Brunch is a real cultural touchstone for many newcomers and an easy first meeting. Nobody has to commit their whole evening and nobody has to drink.
formats.name: Coffee chats and brunch
formats.inChina: Coffee here is a fast transaction and brunch crowds exist mainly in the biggest cities, so it carries less weight than it does at home. Useful as a gentle entry, weak as a centerpiece.
formats.tagline: A low-commitment first step rather than the main event.
formats.soloNote: Sitting in a cafe with people you have not met yet costs you an hour and nothing else.

formats.why: Smaller groups, tighter bonds, and much better suited to people who already know a few faces. Photography walks in particular give you something to look at together, which takes the pressure off the conversation.
formats.name: Interest groups: books, photography, film
formats.inChina: Retention more than recruitment. It matters once somebody has settled in and wants a reason to keep showing up.
formats.tagline: What keeps people coming back rather than what brings them in.
formats.soloNote: Joining alone is fine, though these work better once you already recognize somebody in the room.

whyJoin: Instantly tap into a growing network of expats and globally-minded locals, saying goodbye to loneliness in China.
Experience Chinese culture firsthand with a crew that guides you through food, fun and discovery.
Unlock practical living guides on renting, healthcare, banking setups and mobile payments, written from first-hand experience.
Meet up in person in Guangzhou and Shenzhen, or join the conversation from anywhere in China through our online and national groups.
Build lasting international friendships and a strong sense of belonging with your crew in China.
Be part of a dynamic, open and diverse crew that champions inclusion and celebrates global diversity.

services.title: Organization of Social Activities
points: Parties and socials: rooftop parties, BBQs, karaoke nights, wine tastings and club nights
Networking mixers, food crawls and shared meals, hikes, sports leagues and weekend getaways
Board games and trivia nights, coffee and brunch, interest groups like books, photography and film
services.summary: We organize and share social events across China, so no expat has to spend a weekend sitting at home. Ten formats sit on the board: from rooftop parties, BBQs, karaoke nights, wine tastings and club nights to networking mixers, food crawls, hikes, sports leagues and weekend getaways. We pick the place, set the time and gather the crew; all you have to do is turn up.

services.title: Cultural Experience Activities
points: Tea ceremony, explained by someone who grew up with it
Museum and temple visits with somebody explaining what you are actually looking at
services.summary: Culture workshops are the ones that need organizing before anything happens, and that is exactly why they are worth doing with a crew. Interest in Chinese culture is common; acting on it alone is harder, because you have to find someone who teaches it, get to the right part of town and then work out what you are looking at. A workshop handles all three.

services.title: Chinese Language Exchange and Learning
points: Language exchange meetups with tandem partners
Everyday Mandarin for the things you do in your first month
Structured practice rather than an open room where nobody talks to anyone new
Sessions shaped around a topic instead of free-form mingling
Mandarin and Cantonese practice in a supportive environment
services.summary: Language exchange puts expats who want Mandarin next to locals who want English, and it gives anyone a stated reason to turn up.

services.title: Daily Crew Communication
points: Healthcare: comparing international clinics and health insurance with people who use them
Housing: comparing districts, rents and lease terms before you sign
Banking and mobile payments: walking each other through WeChat Pay and Alipay setup
Other paperwork people get stuck on: driving license conversion and moving pets
services.summary: Online groups where expats swap first-hand answers about daily life in China: housing, healthcare, banking, mobile payments and everything in between. Peer advice from people who have already done it, not a service desk.

orgMethods: Co-creation and execution through third-party partnerships: partner events are planned for later, with the GFIC Crew team providing organizational support.
Initiation and execution by community members: the GFIC Crew team offers organizational support and collaboration.
Initiation, planning and execution by the GFIC Crew team: the team takes the lead in organizing and carrying out events.
refundTerms: Once paid membership opens: anyone who has not joined an activity in their first week and has not broken the community rules can leave and get the fee back in full. There is no fee to refund today, because every group is free to join.
